Four short irregular verbs

These four verbs are short, very common and irregular. Look first at voi: fate and dite are shorter than you'd expect from the infinitive (no \"facete\", no \"dicete\"), and there are a few other surprises.

faredirestaredare
iofacciodicostodo
tufaidicistaidai
lui / leifadicestadà
noifacciamodiciamostiamodiamo
voifateditestatedate
lorofannodiconostannodanno

The rule in one sentence: dire keeps the stem dic- everywhere except voi (dite), fare takes facc- only with io and noi (faccio, facciamo), and stare and dare are conjugated like very short -are verbs (with a double n in loro: stanno, danno).

Pronunciation: dico and dicono are said with a [k] sound; dici, dice, diciamo with a [ch] sound as in \"church\", because c before i or e is pronounced \"ch\". Faccio sounds like \"FAHT-cho\".

The trap: dà (he/she gives) takes an accent, so you don't confuse it with the preposition da you already know: \"Vado da Marco\" (I'm going to Marco's place), but \"Marco dà un libro a Sara\" (Marco gives Sara a book). Do, fa, sta have no accent.

", "

Everyday expressions

With fare (to do, to make), Italian often uses \"do\" where English says \"have\", \"take\" or \"go\".

ItalianEnglish
fare colazioneto have breakfast (no article)
fare la docciato take a shower
fare la spesato go grocery shopping
fare una passeggiatato take a walk
fare sportto play sports, to exercise (no article)
fare un regalo a…to give a gift to…

The weather: Italian has no word for \"it\" in front of the verb. You just say fa (literally \"makes\").

Che tempo fa? Oggi fa molto freddo.What's the weather like? Today it's very cold.

Stare: how you are, and staying

Stare is used to say how you're doing and to say that you're staying somewhere: Come stai? Sto bene. / Stasera sto a casa. To describe someone, keep essere: sono stanco (I'm tired), not \"sto stanco\".

Oggi Sara non sta bene e sta a casa.Today Sara isn't feeling well, and she's staying home.

Dire and dare: a + the person

The person always comes with a (to): dico a Marco (I tell Marco), do il numero di telefono a Giulia (I give Giulia the phone number). English can drop \"to\"; Italian never drops it. Also remember dire di sì, dire di no (to say yes, to say no) and dare una mano (to give a hand).

A ready-made phrase to learn as is: Come si dice « fork » in italiano? (How do you say \"fork\" in Italian?)

title: Fare, dire, stare, dare
topic: present tense of fare, dire, stare, dare and their expressions
why: Second lesson of the unit on verbs used all the time: the learner needs time on common verbs, and fare, dire, stare, dare come up in every everyday conversation. The lesson reuses andare, venire, uscire (including escono, one of the learner's real mistakes) and the preposition da before a person.
